panels.assertion_heading: The strongest version has a number, and the route stays closed
panels.narration: Overnight, we put 1 rotating-parent paper on trial, then built the surviving idea's strongest version ourselves. This is Duho's personal side-interest, not a NebulaMind research programme. The paper's dark-energy route fails its own numbers twice. The rebuilt galaxy-spin route reaches only 0.027 standard deviations with every observable galaxy. The idea's best version now exists on the record with its own number, and the number says the route stays closed.

panels.assertion_heading: The trial checked 23 claims and left 1 symmetry idea standing
panels.narration: We audited arXiv:1910.10819 version 2 claim by claim. Of 23 verdicts, 8 checked out, 4 were errors, 6 were unsupported, 3 were fitted after the observations, 1 was unfalsifiable as stated, and 1 lay outside this audit. The surviving physical core is narrow: if the universe has a preferred spin axis, clockwise and counterclockwise galaxy counts might differ. The paper supplies no trustworthy size for that difference.

panels.assertion_heading: Dark energy puts the paper on both horns of a billion-fold dilemma
panels.narration: The paper identifies cosmic spin with observed dark energy. Follow that statement forward, and dark energy requires rotation at 0.828 times the cosmic expansion rate: 1.09 billion times above the generous Planck rotation bound, and 17.6 billion times above the tighter Saadeh bound. Follow it backward instead, enforcing the generous bound, and rotation supplies less than 1 billion-billionth of observed dark energy. The text provides no third reading.

panels.assertion_heading: Its conserved spin behaves like radiation, not dark energy
panels.narration: A second failure is independent of the first. The paper says the universe conserves angular momentum as it expands. That premise makes the spin fade with the square of cosmic growth, so its proposed rotational energy thins exactly like radiation. On the paper's own terms, the result cannot accelerate the universe. It also lies about 46 standard deviations from the dark-energy measurement the paper cites as support. The claims fail; the author is not the target.

panels.assertion_heading: We rebuilt only the survivor as a strict, frozen model
panels.narration: Rather than rescue the failed sectors, we discarded them. The strict model keeps 1 object: a small, axis-carrying cosmic vorticity on an expanding universe. It begins with a Kerr parent black hole, an inheritance knob from 0 to 1, and 10 numbered assumptions, A0 through A9. No rotating global frame, centrifugal dark energy, or unsupported metric correction returns through the back door. Unknown bounce transfer stays named, not hidden.

panels.assertion_heading: Cosmic expansion erases spin in 2 different stages
panels.narration: The spin-fade law was derived from a pinned vector-perturbation equation and checked by machine algebra. During radiation domination, rotation falls in inverse proportion to cosmic size. During matter and dark-energy domination, it falls with the inverse square. The inflation-era rate has no pinned source, so it remains an explicit parameter rather than a claimed result. Mapping today's microwave-background limit back to galaxy spin-up changes the allowance by only a factor of a few, not enough to rescue it.

panels.assertion_heading: The missing transfer coefficient is now derived and bracketed
panels.narration: Next came the missing bridge: how much galaxy handedness appears per unit of leftover cosmic spin. Combining tidal-torque growth, turnaround, halo spin statistics, and a coherent rotational push gives a transfer coefficient of about 7.2, with an honest bracket from 1.4 to 12.8. Machine algebra reproduced the coefficient and its bounds. Our local novelty check found no printed analytic transfer function of this kind. The strict model still awaits external theorist review before any publication claim.

panels.assertion_heading: The strict answer is 0.027 standard deviations across the whole sky
panels.narration: Now the confrontation is direct. At the generous rotation bound and the fiducial galaxy turnaround time, the predicted handedness imbalance is 1.9 parts in 100 million. Even counting all 2 trillion observable galaxies yields only 0.027 standard deviations. A 3-standard-deviation detection would need about 25 quadrillion galaxies: roughly 12,000 observable universes. Favorable choices across the full bracket reach at most 0.08 standard deviations. No survey lever closes that gap.

panels.assertion_heading: The strict calculation strengthens the earlier closure and constrains the parent
panels.narration: The earlier generous estimate needed 18 observable universes. The derived model needs about 12,000, landing inside the old declared bracket but 25 times below its generous edge. The same chain also turns the microwave-background limit around: inherited parent spin must be diluted by more than 10 to the power 22 for a supermassive parent, or 10 to the power 30 for a stellar parent. That constraint is real but weak: it rules out too little dilution, not parent spin itself.

panels.assertion_heading: Taking the idea seriously means accepting its bounded verdict
panels.narration: We did not prove black-hole-universe cosmology false, and we did not audit every member of that wider family. We tested 1 rotating-parent paper, preserved its bare symmetry idea, froze the strongest explicit model we could justify, derived the missing transfer, and pushed every uncertain lever in its favor. The result is stronger than the earlier generous closure. The idea's best version now exists on the record with its own number, and the number says the route stays closed.
